**The Weight of a Single Leaf**

I remember the first time I noticed how much a single leaf could weigh. It was in the autumn of my childhood, when the maples in our backyard turned from green to gold, then to brown, then to nothing at all. My father had taught me to balance a fallen leaf on the tip of my finger, to feel the delicate curve of its veins, the way it would shiver and fall if I didn’t hold it just right.

One evening, I decided to test its weight. I placed the leaf on a small scale—just a cheap kitchen one—and pressed down. The needle barely moved. A fraction of a gram. But the way it felt in my hand was different. It wasn’t just weight; it was memory. The way it had clung to the branch, the way it had danced in the wind, the way it had whispered secrets to the ground before it let go.

I thought about how much weight we carry—emotions, regrets, the stories we tell ourselves. Some things are light, like a leaf on a breeze. Others are heavy, like a stone in your pocket. But even the heaviest things can be held for a moment, if you know how.

And sometimes, the lightest things are the ones that change everything.
